newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian opposition on top in local elections.
newsitem.headline: Italian opposition on top in local elections.

text.p: Italy's main opposition alliance gave Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left coalition a bloody nose in the weekend's major local elections, according to early results released on Monday.

The centre-right Freedom Alliance was ahead in the mayoral race in Milan after the first round of voting, ending the separatist Northern League's control of the business capital. The Alliance was also winning in the key northern city of Turin.

Prodi's ruling Olive Tree coalition was a distant second in both races, leaving it at the mercy of its parliamentary ally, the hard-left Communist Refoundation, which stood alone in many of the local constituencies and secured strong support.
The elections for mayors and local councils in more than 1,100 towns and cities was the first big test for Prodi and his backers since they triumphed in last April's general election.
"A year later, and the Olive Tree has paid the price. It has not just lost a few leaves, but whole branches," La Repubblica newspaper said in a front page editorial.

The government's popularity has suffered in recent months from resentment at tax hikes it has brought in to cut the budget deficit and try to squeeze Italy into the first wave of countries to join Europe's planned single currency.
Prodi and other leading government figures declined to comment on Sunday's election and were waiting for the full result.
Counting from the vote, for which 9.4 million voters -- or about one-fifth of the national electorate -- were eligible, began early on Monday with final results due later in the day.
A run-off will be held on May 11 between the two leading contenders for mayor in places where no candidate obtains an absolute majority.

With more than a third of the votes counted in the northern powerhouse Milan, industrialist Gabriele Albertini of the Freedom Alliance was ahead with 41.5 percent of the vote against 27.8 percent for Aldo Fumagalli of the Olive Tree.
Milan's outgoing mayor Marco Formentini, elected in 1993 at the height of the League's popularity, came in a poor third with just 19.4 percent of the vote.
The result marked a serious blow to the prestige of the Northern League and a further sign of waning support for its separatist agenda.
League leader Umberto Bossi sought to brush off Formentini's defeat and a poor showing in Turin, saying southern Italian "immigrants" in the cities would never vote for his party.
He said he would advise supporters to "go to the mountains" for the second round and not back anyone in the run-offs.

Although the Olive Tree lost ground in many areas, its candidates were well ahead in the northeastern cities of Trieste and Pordenone, in the Adriatic port of Ancona and in Reggio Calabria on the toe of Italy.
And initial results suggested that the centre-left might still gain control of both Turin and Milan by linking up with its awkward allies, Communist Refoundation.
Refoundation candidates in the wealthy cities of Milan and Turin took around eight and 10 percent of the vote repectively.

"The Olive Tree has now got to ask us for our votes," Refoundation chairman Armando Cossutta told reporters. "We won't give our votes for free...this result shows that Refoundation counts, it counts a lot," he added.
